clue.text: Trick nurse in debate

parts.note: a con is a swindle, the trick a confidence man works
to nurse the sick is to tend them, to look after them

explanation.surface: Somebody playing a trick on a nurse in the middle of an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are verbs dressed as nouns: 'Trick' looks like the thing done and 'nurse' like the person it was done to. Read them as instructions instead and the charade falls out.
explanation.definitionFit: To contend is to argue a case against somebody, which is what the two sides of a debate do.

clue.text: Embrace seal

definitions.meaning: the boxing ring's word for the tight grip two fighters take on each other, which stretches to any close hug
what a negotiator does to a deal when it is settled past all argument

explanation.surface: A hug for a seal.
explanation.walkthrough: Two verbs with nothing at all between them is the shape of a double definition. The animal is the trap, and it is a noun where the clue wants a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A clinch is the boxer's tight hold and so an embrace, while to clinch an agreement is to seal it beyond reopening.

clue.text: Peer into US city — almost

indicators.note: Going into a thing puts you inside it, so the piece named first is planted in the middle of the one named next.

parts.note: NY is the two-letter short form of New York
an earl is a peer of the realm, a rank of the British nobility

explanation.surface: Taking a long look into an American city from just outside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' reads as the verb the sentence needs and is really the nobleman. British ranks are a standing supply of short words: earl, duke, peer.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearly and almost are interchangeable: each says a thing came within a little of happening and then fell short.

clue.text: Former lover on course with worker going beyond the usual limits

parts.note: an ex is the partner somebody used to have
an orbit is the course a satellite runs round its planet
the crossword's standing worker is the ant, one of the colony's labourers

explanation.surface: An old flame on a training course with a colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole tail of the clue, which is why no single word in it looks like a synonym. 'Worker' is the ant nine times in ten; 'bee' is the other one.
explanation.definitionFit: Exorbitant prices go past any reasonable ceiling, and the word's Latin root says the same thing: out of the orbit.

clue.text: Greek letter infidel taxman conceals

indicators.note: To conceal is to hide, and what is hidden here lies unbroken inside the words in front of it.

parts.note: five letters running on across the gap: infiDEL TAxman

explanation.surface: An unbeliever keeping something back from the tax collector.
explanation.walkthrough: The two nouns were picked for their letters rather than their sense, which is why an unbeliever and a tax collector are keeping company at all. The same word is D in the radio alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Delta is the fourth letter of the Greek alphabet, written as the triangle Δ.

clue.text: Walk back then jump into retail unit

indicators.note: Going back is going the other way, so the letters just named are written in the reverse of the order they come in.

parts.note: a step is a single pace of a walk, and turned round it reads PETS
a hop is a short jump

explanation.surface: Retracing your steps and then hopping into a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retail unit' is estate-agent language, deliberately colourless, and it keeps the animals out of sight until the last moment. Only 'back' is an instruction; 'then' and 'into' just join.
explanation.definitionFit: A pet shop is a retail unit — one shop trading from a single unit in a parade or a centre.

clue.text: One travelling quietly with idiot, engineer and old Queen

parts.note: p is piano on a sheet of music, the instruction to play quietly
an ass is a fool, the donkey used as an insult
Eng is the usual short form of engineer on a job title
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the cypher stamped on British postboxes for a queen now gone

explanation.surface: A quiet traveller in the company of a fool, an engineer and an elderly queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' is doing real work: the cypher belongs to a monarch no longer on the throne. Four pieces with only commas and 'and' to mark the joins is the Quiptic's gentlest shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A passenger is the one who rides in the vehicle without driving it, so 'one travelling' names them exactly.

clue.text: Food from lorry missing second element

indicators.note: What is missing is not there, so the letter named straight after it never appears in the word.

parts.note: a lorry is a truck
an element here is a letter, and the second one along is the R that drops out

explanation.surface: Food carried by a lorry that has lost one of its parts.
explanation.walkthrough: Tuck is British schoolchildren's word for food, sold at the school tuck shop. 'Element' sounds chemical and means nothing grander than a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuck is food in British school slang — the sweets, buns and crisps a tuck shop sells.

clue.text: Run off after domestic pest

indicators.note: What comes after a thing is written behind it, so the piece named first in the clue is the second one down.

parts.note: house does the work of domestic in house cat, house plant and housework
to fly is to flee, to run off at speed

explanation.surface: Bolting off in pursuit of some household nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' is the instruction and not a mere join, which is what puts the running-off at the end rather than the start. The creature is domestic in the plainest sense: it lives indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: A housefly is a pest in the everyday sense — an insect that gets inside, settles on food and is entirely unwanted.

clue.text: Rule out putting contralto in overture

indicators.note: A thing that is in another sits inside it, so the letter named before goes within the word named after.

parts.note: a prelude is the piece played to open a work, an overture
C is the score's mark for the contralto voice, as S is soprano and T tenor

explanation.surface: A contralto being slipped into the orchestra's opening number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rule out' opens like a sentence about somebody making a ruling, and it is the definition. Voice parts are a quiet source of single letters in music clues.
explanation.definitionFit: To preclude something is to make it impossible before it can happen, which is to rule it out.

clue.text: One possessed flipping love for state

indicators.note: To flip a thing is to turn it over, so the piece beside it comes out with its letters the other way round.

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
somebody who possessed a thing had it, and HAD turned over reads DAH
love is the tennis score of nothing, written as a nought

explanation.surface: A person possessed, going wild over love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' is the mild British swear word in the surface and a turn-round order in the wordplay. Love has meant nil on a tennis scoreboard for well over a century.
explanation.definitionFit: Idaho is one of the fifty United States, so the bare word 'state' defines it by example.

clue.text: Mislaid reason for hopeless endeavour

parts.note: something mislaid has been lost
the reason a thing happened is its cause

explanation.surface: Nobody can now remember why the doomed attempt was made in the first place.
explanation.walkthrough: Two ordinary synonyms happen to sit side by side as a set phrase, so the work is all in spotting where four letters end and five begin. The phrase began as a political or military one: a side already beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: A lost cause is an endeavour that can no longer come off, which is what makes it hopeless.

clue.text: Feted rebel acted out

indicators.note: Letters described as out are out of their proper order and have to be set down afresh.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A much-admired rebel throwing a tantrum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acted out' is the psychologist's phrase for a tantrum, which is what holds the surface together; only the last word is the instruction, and the one before it is material.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody celebrated is publicly honoured and talked about, which is what being feted amounts to.

clue.text: Endlessly touches fish

indicators.note: Something without ends loses them at both sides, so the first and last letters of the word named next are dropped.

parts.note: one who touches a thing feels it, and the word gives up its F and its S

explanation.surface: Somebody who will not stop prodding a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' here strips both ends, not just the tail, which is the one liberty the clue takes. The three-letter fish of crosswords is nearly always this one, worth writing in before any crossing arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: An eel is a fish — the long snake-bodied kind that lives in rivers and the sea.

clue.text: Savage crossing hill and winning

indicators.note: To cross something is to go over it from one side to the other, so the word doing the crossing lies across the piece named next and takes it in.

parts.note: a savage dog is a vicious one
a tor is a bare rocky hill, the word used on Dartmoor and across the West Country

explanation.surface: A brute going over a hill and coming off best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Savage' reads as the noun starting a sentence and is wanted as an adjective. Tor is worth filing away: three letters, and the setter's favourite hill.
explanation.definitionFit: To be victorious is to have won, so the adjective sits exactly where 'winning' does.

clue.text: Resolute way Ron grimaced at first then left

parts.note: St is the abbreviation a map or an address uses for street
the name written straight into the answer

indicators.note: What comes at first is the opening, so only the first letter of the word in front of it is taken.

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
money left to a nephew has been willed to him

explanation.surface: Ron pulling a face and then walking out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' is the trap: it reads as departure and means bequeathed, the sense a solicitor uses. 'Way' is street, which every map shortens to two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody strong-willed holds to their purpose under pressure, which is what resolute describes.

clue.text: Artist welcomed by poorest miserable machinists

indicators.note: A guest welcomed by a host is taken in, so these two letters join the letters of the word that welcomes them.
Something miserable is in a sorry state and out of sorts, and letters out of sorts are letters out of order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
an RA is a Royal Academician, the letters a painter puts after their name

explanation.surface: A painter taken in by the poorest and most wretched of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miserable' sits beside 'poorest' as though describing the same wretched crowd, and it is the instruction. Two letters welcomed into seven makes nine, which is the length wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: An operator is somebody who works a machine for a living, which is what a machinist does all day.

clue.text: Warn in notice — day is hot

parts.note: a notice placed in a paper is an ad
Mon is the three letters a diary prints for Monday
the word taken straight from the clue
H is the letter on the hot tap

explanation.surface: A notice in the paper saying that the day will be a hot one.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash does the work of a colon, so everything after it is building material. Days of the week give three letters apiece — Mon, Tue, Wed — and the bare word 'day' is enough to ask for one.
explanation.definitionFit: To admonish somebody is to reprove them and tell them not to do it again, a warning delivered face to face.

clue.text: Upsetting details about duck being detached

indicators.note: To upset a thing is to tip it over and spill what is in it, leaving the contents in no particular order.
What goes about a thing is taken round it, so this letter joins the ones beside it rather than standing apart.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
a batsman out for no runs has scored a duck, written as a nought

explanation.surface: Distressing information about a duck that had wandered off on its own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upsetting' reads as distressing and means overturned. A duck is cricket's score of nothing, drawn as an O, and it is the steadiest single letter in the language of clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Something isolated stands apart from everything round it, which is to be detached from the rest.

clue.text: Strangely design attire to fall apart

indicators.note: Letters described as strangely arranged are not in the arrangement they should be, so they are set down in another order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters

explanation.surface: Oddly designing clothes that are meant to come to pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator sits straight in front of its material, and the material is exactly as long as the answer. Counting the letters before you shuffle them is the habit that makes long anagrams quick.
explanation.definitionFit: A thing that disintegrates comes apart into its separate pieces, which is to fall apart.

clue.text: Cause harm to barrier over time

indicators.note: One thing over another is above it, and in a down entry above means written first.

parts.note: a dam is the barrier thrown across a river
an age is a long stretch of time

explanation.surface: The slow harm that years of weather do to a barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over time' reads as one phrase meaning gradually, and the wordplay breaks it in two so that 'over' can stack one piece on the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To damage a thing is to cause harm to it — the same action in one word instead of three.

clue.text: Hunted and restrained we hear

indicators.note: What we hear is a sound, so the word wanted is the one this sounds like rather than the one spelt out.

parts.note: somebody chaste is restrained, holding back from sex, and the two spellings are said the same way

explanation.surface: Somebody pursued and then held back.
explanation.walkthrough: Two past participles side by side look like one police report, which is what hides the join. The pair are perfect homophones in British English, differing only on the page.
explanation.definitionFit: To chase is to hunt, to run after something that is getting away, so the past tenses match too.

clue.text: Bird not following predator

indicators.note: 'Not' cancels what comes after it, so the letter named there is absent from what is left.

parts.note: fowl is the old word for a bird, still alive in wildfowl and fowling
f. is the footnote's abbreviation for following, and it is the letter cancelled

explanation.surface: A bird that will not trail after a predator.
explanation.walkthrough: F for following comes from footnotes, where p.12f means page 12 and the page after it. The bird in the wordplay and the bird in the definition are two different birds.
explanation.definitionFit: An owl hunts and kills mice and voles by night, which makes it a predator.

clue.text: Rubbish black tree and dead tree

parts.note: B is the grade stamped on a soft black pencil
the alder is a waterside tree of British riverbanks
d for died, the letter a family tree puts before the date
the ash is one of the commonest British hardwoods

explanation.surface: A gardener dismissing two trees, one blackened and one dead, as worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: Two trees in one clue is the cue to reach for the short ones — ash, elm, yew, alder — rather than anything exotic. The letters for black and dead come from pencils and gravestones.
explanation.definitionFit: Balderdash is nonsense, the Victorian word for the rubbish somebody talks.

clue.text: Force dropping uniform clothing

indicators.note: To drop something is to let go of it, so the letter named next falls out of the word that holds it.

parts.note: duress is force used to make somebody act against their will
uniform is U in the radio alphabet, and it is the letter let go

explanation.surface: A police force doing away with its uniforms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force dropping uniform' reads as one phrase about a change of kit, which is exactly what hides the split. The radio alphabet — alpha, bravo, charlie — supplies single letters for words too ordinary to abbreviate.
explanation.definitionFit: Dress is clothing in the collective sense — evening dress, national dress — as well as the single garment.

clue.text: Group of players principally taking roles in operetta

indicators.note: The principal letter of a word is the one it begins with, so each word after this gives up its first only.

parts.note: the opening letters of the four words in order

explanation.surface: Performers taking the chief parts in an operetta.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Principally' is doing the work of chiefly, and a word's chief letter is its first. The operetta is scenery: the answer holds for any three players, on a stage or a pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: A trio is three people performing together, most often musicians, which makes it a group of players.

clue.text: Bury Post Office initially send everything to place inbetween

parts.note: to inter a body is to bury it

indicators.note: What happens initially happens at the start, so only the starting letter of each word that follows is wanted.

parts.note: PO is the Post Office's own abbreviation, as in PO Box
the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Burying a request the Post Office was asked to send on in full.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' governs the two words after it, not the Post Office in front, which needs no cutting because PO is its own short form. Inter is the undertaker's verb: a body is interred.
explanation.definitionFit: To interpose is to put something in between two others — a remark, an objection, a body.

clue.text: Duck hit revolving stones

indicators.note: Something revolving turns right round, so the piece beside it comes out with its letters running backwards.

parts.note: a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, written as a nought
a slap is a hit, and turned round it reads PALS

explanation.surface: A duck taking a hit from some spinning rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: The stones are gemstones rather than rubble, which is the whole of the misdirection. 'Duck' is cricket's nought and the crossword's most dependable O.
explanation.definitionFit: An opal is a precious stone, the milky one that flashes colour as it is turned in the light.

clue.text: Revolting rogue regularly wearing animal skins

indicators.note: Letters taken regularly are taken at a fixed interval, every second one along.

parts.note: a hide is an animal's skin, the thing a tanner works on

indicators.note: Clothes go on outside the person wearing them, so the letters doing the wearing sit inside the ones named next.

parts.note: every second letter of rOgUe

explanation.surface: A crook going about dressed in furs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' is the definition and has nothing to do with rebellion here. When a clue says regularly, check the odd letters as well as the even ones before settling.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hideous is ugly enough to turn the stomach, which is to be revolting to look at.

clue.text: Hold up pay out across America

indicators.note: Something laid across another spans it from side to side, so the word named first goes round the one named next.

parts.note: to spend is to pay money out
US is the United States' own abbreviation

explanation.surface: A raid on money being handed out across America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold up' is the robber's phrase in the surface and the rope's in the answer: what is held up hangs from above.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspend an object is to hang it so something above holds it up, and to suspend a process is to hold that up too.
